title: FPTR Scheduler · Joint Beam and Resource Scheduling
description: FPTR applies feasibility-preserving transactional refinement to deadline-aware joint beam and resource scheduling.
problemPageDescription: The six coupled constraint families in joint beam and resource scheduling, and the timeout risk of mutating the live solution.
methodPageDescription: FPTR's feasibility-preserving transactional refinement, four commit checks, and cumulative 87 ms stage chain.
evidencePageDescription: FPTR stage gains, budget–quality trade-offs, runtime distributions, stress tests, and exact calibration.
reproducePageDescription: Build, run, and independently validate FPTR, then reproduce its public experiments.
demoPageDescription: Run the repository's real FPTR C++17 joint beam and resource scheduler directly in your browser.
homeSubtitle: Deadline-constrained joint beam and resource scheduling
paperThesis: Keep a feasible solution. Refine in isolation. Commit after validation.
heroCaption: One bounded run: the feasible incumbent is always releasable, and a candidate takes effect only after the transactional gate.
heroArtAlt: An intelligent base station coordinates resource blocks along a deadline path
snapshotProblemBody: Beams, resources, buffers, and deadlines jointly determine legality.
snapshotMethodBody: A candidate commits only when complete, timely, valid, and better.
snapshotResultBody: The full configuration improves quality while meeting the 100 ms external deadline.
releaseShort: Public code and an executable Demo; research claims remain tied to the paper artifacts.
problemBody: Beam choices change available rates, resource memberships shape sharing, and finite buffers change the real value of every move. A local edit can easily invalidate an otherwise legal allocation.
systemModelBody: The paper defines user, resource, subband, and beam sets. Each user has a finite buffer, base link quality, and per-beam capability. Each resource explicitly belongs to one or two subbands, and a two-member set need not be adjacent.
objectiveBody: Equation (6) clips traffic at each user's finite buffer before summing deliverable traffic. An output has positive utility only if it passes every constraint and is serialized before the external deadline.
trafficMapBody: This step function is a deterministic one-snapshot traffic abstraction, not a continuous physical-layer rate law.
problemAsideBody: When refinements mutate the live solution, a timeout or failed validation can leave only a partial result. FPTR isolates candidates, so a failed attempt costs that attempt—not the usable incumbent.
scenarioQuestionTitle: What must the scheduler answer each cycle?
scenarioQuestionBody: Which subband-beam pairs to activate and which users to place on every resource. The result must be completely serialized before the deadline and satisfy every constraint.
constraintBody: Radio activation determines available capability, resource sharing determines legal combinations, and the delivery contract applies finite buffers and a hard deadline to the complete output.
mutatingBody: Local edit → constraints not yet repaired → time expires → the current solution cannot be released.
transactionBody: Keep the incumbent → finish and validate a private candidate → commit it as a whole or discard it as a whole.
methodBody: FPTR keeps an incumbent—the current releasable feasible solution—and builds each candidate in isolated state. Only four passing checks replace it; any failure leaves the current allocation untouched.
topSSummary: For a fixed sharing cardinality, selecting users with the largest marginal gains solves the local query exactly.
topSBody: With the beam mask, resource, retained capacity, and sharing cardinality fixed, the sharing penalty depends only on that cardinality. Selecting the largest user marginals solves the local query exactly.
invariantSummary: At every stage boundary, the incumbent remains a legal solution ready for release.
invariantBody: If the empty fallback is feasible and the validator is sound, rejection leaves the incumbent unchanged and acceptance must pass independent validation. The current allocation is therefore feasible after every gate and before serialization.
reference: BeamFirst is an independent reference method and is not part of the cumulative chain.
incumbentBody: The current best feasible solution, already fully checked and ready to serialize.
gateBody: Checks completeness, timing, legality, and strict improvement together.
methodLimitSummary: FPTR guarantees feasibility and monotone improvement, but not global optimality or a fixed approximation ratio.
methodLimitBody: FPTR promises an always-releasable feasible incumbent and accepts only strict improvements. It does not provide a global-optimality or fixed approximation-ratio guarantee.
evidenceBody: Five research questions examine quality, deadline behavior, compatibility-group stress, matched external baselines, and exact optimality calibration.

rq2Question: Is the quality gain bought by missing the deadline?
rq2Body: All 750 full-configuration (Full) runs passed independent validation, and every end-to-end wall-clock time stayed below 100 ms. The 87 ms value is the internal algorithm budget; the median and 95th-percentile times (p50/p95) and worst case include startup and I/O, so they may exceed 87 ms: 60.28, 87.29, and 92.14 ms.
runtimeCaption: Empirical cumulative distribution (ECDF) of solver wall-clock time under the 87 ms internal budget. The 100 ms dashed line is the external crediting deadline.
budgetCaption: Raising the budget from 60 to 87 ms moves average gain from 1.60% to 1.65%, indicating diminishing returns.
rq3Question: Do quality and runtime remain stable as compatibility groups grow?
rq3Body: The compatibility-group (CG) stress suite changes group size and coverage together. The full configuration remains positive while 95th-percentile wall-clock time is reported alongside quality.

rq4Question: How does Full compare under matched budgets and crediting rules?
rq4Body: Under the common 87 ms internal budget and 100 ms external crediting rule, the full configuration (Full) gains 6.58%–8.40% on average over six independent search implementations.
rq4Qualifier: This comparison covers six independent implementations in this repository under the same budget and validation rules; it is not a universal ranking of published solvers.
optimalityCaption: The gate guarantees feasibility and strict improvement, not proximity to the global optimum. The wider case exposes that boundary.
protocolDetails: Open the full protocol and counting rules
protocolLead: The same inputs, objective, and validator are used, with zero credit for late results.
protocolBody: The single-threaded C++17 scheduler was compiled with g++ 13.3 and -O2, then run on Linux 6.8 with a 2.30 GHz Xeon E5-2686 v4. External wall time covers process launch through output collection. Nonzero exits, illegal outputs, or runs above 100 ms receive zero utility, and an independent Python validator recomputes the objective.
baselineBody: The programs share the input-output contract, objective, and validation procedure, but do not call FPTR core code. The result is bounded to this model, host, and implementation family; it is not a universal ranking of published solvers.
limitsBody: The evaluation uses synthetic static instances, one unpinned host, and a small exact suite. It does not yet cover dynamic queues, fairness, mobility, richer interference, continuous precoding, or deployment traces.
evidenceNote: Code-only public release. Current figures are audited PNG fallbacks; claims remain tied to the paper artifacts.

rq5Body: The full configuration (Full) reaches the global optimum in 8 of 12 independently calibrated dynamic-programming cases. The median, mean, and maximum gaps are 0%, 3.19%, and 25%.

equation1Lead: The resource span is the inclusive distance from its first to last member.
equation1Aria: Equation 1: d sub r equals the maximum of T sub r minus its minimum plus one
equation2Lead: Total activations obey the global budget; every nonempty resource activates at least one beam on each member subband.
equation2Aria: Equation 2: global beam budget and resource activation constraints
equation3Lead: The empty set and singletons are always legal; multi-user sharing must lie entirely inside one compatibility group.
equation3Aria: Equation 3: compatibility-group feasible domain for a resource user set
equation4Lead: Selected capability sums active beams only on member subbands and normalizes by the membership span.
equation5Lead: Effective link value combines base quality, the sharing-cardinality penalty, and the selected-capability ratio.
equation5Aria: Equation 5: effective link value for a user on a resource
equation6Aria: Equation 6: F of alpha and G is the sum over users of the minimum between user buffer and that user's traffic summed over assigned resources
equation7Aria: Equation 7: maximize F over alpha and G subject to constraints 2 and 3 and binary activations
equation7Note: Constraints (2) and (3) in Equation (7) are the activation budget and legal sharing domain shown above; finite buffers and the hard deadline complete the delivery contract.
equation8Aria: Equation 8: at fixed sharing cardinality s, the marginal gain of user u on resource r is clipped traffic after adding the resource minus the retained clipped traffic
equation8Note: The retained capacity excludes the current resource. Once sharing cardinality is fixed, user marginals are independent, so selecting the largest s terms is optimal.
paperEquationOrderNote: The page follows conceptual order while retaining the paper's equation numbers, so Equation (9) appears before Equation (8).
equation9Aria: Equation 9: replace the incumbent with the candidate if and only if the candidate is complete, validation finishes before the stage cutoff, validation passes, and the objective strictly improves
equation9Note: Finishing candidate construction is insufficient: independent validation must also return before the stage cutoff. Equation (9) excludes partial, expired, illegal, and non-improving candidates.
budgetRuleLead: Stage-cutoff scaling for any internal budget
budgetRuleAria: Stage proportions rho are 45, 60, 70, 78, and 84; tail reserve is 3 milliseconds; cutoff t sub j is B minus the tail reserve, times rho sub j, divided by 84
metricEquationLead: Instance-level statistical unit and relative gain
metricEquationAria: Appendix Equation A1: each instance and method uses the median of five traffic runs; the gain of method A over method B is their median traffic difference divided by method B median traffic
metricEquationNote: Percentages first average instance-level gains within each scenario and then weight the five scenarios equally; they must not be read as a ratio of aggregate mean traffic.
